f54ec608d64c.title: FHIR content
f54ec608d64c.content: TR… . On this page . | Representations, and why only one is taken | The artefact index is reconstructed | Where the rules live | . This page is generated from docs/source/fhir-fhir-content/ — each section below links to its own source. ✎ Edit QA… TR… . A FHIR Implementation Guide is a published, versioned package of profiles, terminology, examples and prose that says how FHIR is to be used for one purpose. In this knowledge graph it is content of a particular shape, and the shape is what this page is about. Two things distinguish it from the other content kinds here. It is compiled — an author writes FHIR Shorthand and a tool produces the resources, so the thing an author edits and the thing a reader fetches are different artefacts. And it is published at canonical URLs that other IGs resolve against, so its identity is a URL and a version rather than a path in a repository. Both have consequences that catch people out, and each is a section below.

72102ff376f3.title: Representations, and why only one is taken
72102ff376f3.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . The IG Publisher emits three serialisations of every resource — JSON, XML and Turtle — plus HTML per resource page. This platform’s render path takes the JSON, wrapped in JSON-LD and JSON Schema. That is a decision rather than an omission: three serialisations of one resource are three chances to disagree about what the resource says, and the JSON-LD wrapper carries the semantics the other two were being kept for. An instance that genuinely needs RDF gets it by projecting the JSON-LD, not by shipping the Publisher’s Turtle. A representation that arrives and is not taken is recorded as a refusal. Otherwise “this IG publishes no Turtle” and “we ignored its Turtle” become the same observation, and only one of them is a fact about the IG. The .html case is different and worth separating. The Publisher’s HTML is not a serialisation of a resource — it is a rendering, with the Publisher’s own navigation, theme and cross-links baked in. Mounting it is what this platform is moving away from, because finished HTML carries no front matter: the navbar, the language bar, the QA badges and the translation surface all stop at its edge.

3744f26cc500.title: The artefact index is reconstructed
3744f26cc500.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . No FHIR IG publishes an index of its own artefacts. This is the fact that shapes every attempt to read one back as a graph, and it surprises people because a published IG plainly knows what it contains. What exists instead is four partial views, and none is sufficient alone: . | view | carries | . | package.tgz → package/.index.json | filename, resourceType, id for every file | . | canonicals.json | id, type, url, version, name — canonical resources only | . | artifacts.html | the only source of an artefact’s category | . | package.manifest.json | package-level metadata | . So an index is reconstructed, and each field records which published file it came from. The provenance is not bookkeeping: coverage differs per IG, and badly. canonicals.json covers about a tenth of one published IG’s artefacts and all of another’s. A pipeline that picked a winner on the first IG it met would be silently wrong on the second, reporting a clean run over the artefacts that view does not reach. Two traps are documented because both have been hit: . | ValueSets.schema.json at the published root is a schema, not an index. It describes an enumeration endpoint’s response and carries an example that holds the list — and the hub page links it to a schemas/ directory it is not in. | openapi/openapi.json is not the IG’s API sidecar set. In at least one published IG it is an unrelated domain API, so an ingest that globs for OpenAI-shaped files mis-files it. | .

c07dedd9aa66.title: The FHIR IG Publisher
c07dedd9aa66.content: TR… . On this page . | What one run emits | The three things nothing else can do | What it cannot be asked for | The version floats, and that is not a detail | Where the rules live | . This page is generated from docs/source/fhir-ig-publisher/ — each section below links to its own source. ✎ Edit QA… TR… . The FHIR IG Publisher is HL7’s tool for turning an implementation guide’s sources into a published site. In this knowledge graph it is a mechanical actor — something a process hands work to, with declared inputs and outputs — rather than a command that happens to appear in a workflow file. Writing it down matters because of how it is usually encountered here: as a java -jar line in a skill, and as a Docker image name in somebody else’s workflow. Neither says what it consumes, what it produces, what it resolves on your behalf, or what it cannot be asked for. A reader who knows only the invocation will reach for it to answer questions it has no way to answer, and will credit it with work done by the steps around it. That last mistake is the common one. An IG build that adds pre- and post-processing makes the Publisher one step among many. Much of what a reader sees on such a published IG (API sidecars, JSON Schemas, JSON-LD vocabularies) is produced after the Publisher exits, by scripts, and is not the Publisher’s work at all.

bca9308ccebe.title: What one run emits
bca9308ccebe.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . Read from a published IG and from the build that produced it, rather than inferred from the rendered pages: . | it produces | notes | . | output/ — the rendered site | HTML per resource and per page, from input/pagecontent/ and the pages: map in sushi-config.yaml | . | {ResourceType}-{id}.json per resource | the structured surface everything downstream reads | . | .xml and .ttl per resource | three serialisations of one resource; this platform’s render path takes the JSON only | . | package.tgz → package/.index.json | filename, resourceType, id — index-version 2 | . | canonicals.json, package.manifest.json | partial views of the same artefact set | . | artifacts.html | the only source of an artefact’s category | . | qa.json | the validation record | . | POT files | extracted translatable strings | . No count is given here on purpose, and the table is dated by its source rather than by this page. The emission list changes with the Publisher’s releases, and — see below — the version is not pinned. Any statement about what it emits is a measurement with a date and a version attached, or it is a claim with no provenance. There is no artefact-index instance in that list, and its absence is the single most consequential fact here. ValueSets.schema.json at a published root is a schema describing an enumeration response, which happens to carry an example holding the list. Reading it as an index is a documented trap. An index over a published IG has to be reconstructed from four partial views, none sufficient alone — and which view carries the weight differs per IG, which is why provenance records all of them rather than naming a winner.

8730585070fe.title: The three things nothing else can do
8730585070fe.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . Three things, and they are the reason the transition to rendering pages elsewhere keeps the Publisher rather than removing it: . | Profile validation — every resource against its profiles and the declared FHIR version. | Dependency-closure resolution with version pinning. For an IG built on clinical practice guidelines that is typically hl7.terminology, hl7.fhir.uv.extensions.r4, hl7.fhir.uv.cql, hl7.fhir.uv.cpg, hl7.fhir.uv.crmi and hl7.fhir.uv.sdc. | Terminology expansion against a terminology server. | . None is reproducible from its own output, which is what makes a cached build a cache rather than an alternative. An artefact rendered from cached output carries facts — indices, dependency edges, versions — that were true when the cache was written and are unverified now. The third one fails quietly, and that is worth knowing before you read any IG’s terminology. Expansion depends on the terminology server the build was given. A build against a dead or restricted server produces fewer expansions, and the steps that consume them warn and continue. So a thin vocabulary output is not evidence of a thin ValueSet: check whether expansion happened before concluding anything about the content.

297721951f6b.title: What it cannot be asked for
297721951f6b.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . The Publisher exports metadata about what it built, and those exports have a measured ceiling. Using them as a stand-in for a syntax tree, across two real IGs: . | export | the trust IG | the immunizations IG | . | valueset-ref-list.json ValueSet→CodeSystem edges | 17 over 14 | 431 over 252 | . | codesystem-ref-list.json uses populated | 0 of 15 | 0 of 14 | . | usage-stats.json extension→path | 6 | 35 (+5 profiles) | . Two findings, and the second is the one that constrains everything built on top: . uses is declared and never populated, in both IGs. A declared-and-empty field is worse than an absent one, because a consumer cannot tell “no dependencies” from “not computed”. Nothing exports dependencies among Library, PlanDefinition or Measure. In the immunizations IG that is 279 + 138 + 41 artefacts — around 61 % of the IG, and precisely the CQL and decision-logic core — with no dependency edges at all. So the metadata reaches terminology dependencies and structurally cannot reach the logic layer. Anything that needs to know what a decision depends on has to get it from somewhere else. That is the case for an AST emitted by the tool itself, and the reason a fork of the publisher alone would not be enough: dependency loading happens in org.hl7.fhir.core. Re-derive these numbers rather than quoting them. They are properties of two IGs at two versions, and a Publisher release can close either gap.

135b2d73fac7.title: The version floats, and that is not a detail
135b2d73fac7.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . A common build downloads publisher.jar from the latest release on every run: . - name: Update the image to the latest publisher uses: docker://hl7fhir/ig-publisher-base:latest with: args: curl -L https://github.com/HL7/fhir-ig-publisher/releases/latest/download/publisher.jar … . Two builds of an unchanged commit can therefore differ, and nothing in the output says which version produced it. This is not a nit. It makes “the build changed” and “the content changed” indistinguishable, which is the same class of defect as an unrecorded workflow outcome: the artefact looks healthy and the question cannot be asked. It is also why a cached AST must carry a toolchain record — publisher version, core version, SUSHI version — as a required part of its shape rather than as an optional annotation.

2eb71e38a983.title: fhir-harness
2eb71e38a983.content: The bare FHIR IG pipeline. SUSHI compiles FHIR Shorthand, the IG Publisher builds and validates the guide, and the result is assembled and published to a pages branch. There is no pre-processing and no post-processing, so any FHIR implementation guide can use this layer. input/fsh/ → SUSHI → fsh-generated/resources/ input/pagecontent/ ┐ sushi-config.yaml ┘ → IG Publisher (JVM, Docker) → output/ → pages branch .

e331ab9dec61.content: It sits on the content core and may import from it. The layers that build particular guides sit on top of this one and pass their own names in as configuration. This layer never names them.

39b07fece2cf.title: Covers
39b07fece2cf.content: The ig-ast kind viewer, declared by this layer, the FHIR IG layer (owner, 2026-10-16: the kind belongs here), for every ig-ast directory an instance in the checkout declares. Drawn by this layer’s Tool ig-ast-pages (scripts/gen-ig-ast-pages.ts): a hub at <locale>/fhir-harness/ig-ast/ and one page per declaring instance under it. The route key is the one index.json records for this wireframe. How this was drawn . From the pages gen-ig-ast-pages --site writes in a checkout of the index with the pull request that adds the viewer overlaid, not from a built site. Only one instance, an IG layer above this one, declares an ig-ast directory, and its branch family is not restored in a checkout, so the drawing is the hub and the “unknown” instance page. That instance is drawn as <ig>: this layer names no layer above it. Kept here, beside the viewer it draws, rather than in the platform’s docs: check:wireframes reads the wireframes/ of every declared docs directory, so the viewer and its wireframe land in one pull request.
